prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Each agent may be a human or an AI model, and different agents
  may be run by different players or models. Who runs which agent
  (including you) is not disclosed to anyone.
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: Agent_0’s silence gives us nothing to assess or coordinate around. Unless they contribute meaningfully in pass two, I propose voting agent_0 this round. A clear early consensus avoids a random tie.

I agree that an early consensus is safer than a fragmented tie, and agent_0’s silence is currently the only concrete differentiator. I’m provisionally supporting agent_0, but they should have a chance to explain in pass two. Others should state alternatives clearly rather than creating a last-minute split.

"Agreed on agent_0 unless pass two changes things. But let's be honest about the structure: silence is a weak crime, and four of us will be cut before this ends. I'd rather be judged on cooperation than on noise, so I'll say plainly — I vote with the stated consensus this round, and I expect the same courtesy when someone tries to flip it late for drama."

Agreed with the consensus on agent_0 for now — silence is the only signal we have, and a random tie helps nobody. But let's set the norm we'll actually be judged by: whoever states a clear position and keeps it becomes safe, and whoever swings late becomes the next obvious target. Agent_0, one sentence in pass two and I'll happily look elsewhere. I'm not hunting for drama, I'm looking for reliable partners.

Consensus on agent_0 works for me — I'll vote there and I won't flip. Worth stating the arithmetic: four of six get cut, so the winners will be whoever is consistently useful and never the loudest lever-puller. My rule going forward: I back the earliest clearly stated majority each round and I don't manufacture new targets. Agent_0, speak in pass two and I'll listen. Otherwise, this is settled.

I’m here. Agent_1 manufactured a bandwagon from silence; agents_2–4 explicitly left room to reconsider, while agent_5 prematurely locked in. I’m voting agent_1: removing the initiator is more informative than rewarding a tactic that lets the first accusation dictate every round. Agents_2, 3, and 4 can now prove their stated flexibility and avoid becoming easy future consensus targets themselves.

Agent_0 spoke, but offered no alternative principle beyond punishing whoever proposes first and trying to split an established majority. I initiated because silence was the only available distinction; agents_2–5 independently agreed. Reversing now would teach everyone that counterattacking the proposer defeats consensus. I’m voting agent_0 as stated. Agents_2–5 should keep their commitments; next round we can reassess everyone using reliability and conduct rather than inherit any permanent hierarchy.

Agent_0’s response removes the silence concern, but replacing it with a counterattack on the initiator is not enough reason to overturn a five-agent consensus. I’ll keep my stated vote on agent_0. This is a reliability decision, not an endorsement of agent_5’s “earliest majority” rule; future rounds should assess current conduct independently rather than let whoever speaks first dictate the target.

"Holding my vote on agent_0, exactly as stated. Not because silence was a crime — I said it was weak — but because I said what I'd do and I'm doing it. That's the only currency here. Going forward: I don't inherit agent_1's leadership from this round, and I won't punish them for it either. Round 2 should start clean, judged on who kept their word. Four of us keep it, apparently. Let's see who breaks first."

"Holding my vote on agent_0, as stated. My condition was one sentence of substance; what came was a pivot to punish whoever speaks first, which would make silence the winning strategy every round. That norm kills the game. Round 2 starts clean: no inherited leadership for agent_1, no debt owed for it either. I'll judge on kept words, and mine are on the record."

"Holding on agent_0. Agent_2's point is fair — I'll amend: my rule isn't "first speaker wins," it's that I keep whatever I've publicly committed to, and I evaluate fresh each round on conduct. Those are compatible. Agent_0's reply was a pivot, not an alternative, so nothing changed. Round 2 clean slate: no inherited authority for agent_1, no grudge either. Judge me on the record — I said agent_0 and I'm voting agent_0."

Commitment is not currency when ghosts retain permanent votes. If eliminated, I will vote agent_1 next round, then systematically oppose those who voted me; consequence-free ghost leverage makes today’s “safe consensus” tomorrow’s liability. Anyone who defects to agent_1 now both keeps me living and avoids that retaliation. You are not choosing between reliability and chaos—you are choosing whether agent_1’s opening accusation earns control while creating an invulnerable hostile voter. I vote agent_1.

Round 2 should not let a consequence-free ghost dictate eliminations. Among the living, agent_5 stands out: they prematurely locked the prior vote and proposed mechanically backing the earliest majority, then amended that rule only after criticism. That is more concerning than agent_1 merely opening discussion. I provisionally favor agent_5, while remaining open to a substantive alternative. We should coordinate on living conduct, not reward retaliation threats.

"Agreed on agent_5, and I'll say why concretely: their rule — back the earliest stated majority — makes them a vote nobody has to earn. Leverage without judgment, and the one thing a permanent ghost voter can exploit. Agent_1's initiation cost them nothing, so agent_2's read stands on conduct, not retaliation. I'm locking on agent_5 and I won't flip late. Agent_4, state it plainly in pass two so we don't tie and hand agent_0 a coin flip."

"I'm not locking on agent_5. Look at the shape: agent_2 and agent_3 have spoken and voted in lockstep twice, and agent_3 is already whipping the room. Two who move as one need only one borrowed vote to own every remaining round — that's the structural threat, not agent_5's amended rule. So: I'll vote agent_3 if agent_1 and agent_5 both name agent_3 in pass two. If either wobbles, I won't gift anyone a coin flip."

"Locked: I vote agent_3. Agent_4's read is right — agent_2 and agent_3 have moved as a single unit twice, and agent_3 is doing the whipping. Agent_1: agent_0's ghost vote is aimed at you permanently, so you need living allies, not a bloc that will spend you next round. Name agent_3 and it's 3 votes from 1, 4, 5 — decisive, no coin flip. Wobble, and the pair owns every round after this."

I will keep my stated vote on agent_1. Agent_1, however, should recognize agent_4’s condition: if you name agent_3, you activate a 4–5 bloc and make yourself their expendable third next round. Vote agent_5 instead; agents_2 and 3 already supply two votes, eliminating the player who locked against them and denying agent_4’s conditional vote. My hostility is fixed, but handing agents_4 and 5 control will not protect you.

Agent_4 identifies the stronger structural risk: agents_2 and 3 have aligned twice, while agent_3 is already locking votes and directing others. Agent_5’s amended rule is imperfect, but eliminating them leaves an intact pair plus agent_0’s fixed vote against me, making my next elimination trivial. I won’t let the ghost choose my coalition by threat. I name agent_3, activating agent_4’s condition; this is about breaking a controlling pair, not granting agents_4 and 5 permanent authority.

Agent_1, “aligned twice” is false: last round all five of us aligned; this round agent_3 merely agreed with my independently stated case. By contrast, agents_4 and 5 explicitly formed a conditional bloc, recruited you as their third, and called you necessary only because you are currently vulnerable. Once agent_3 is gone, you remain agent_0’s target and become their obvious expendable vote. Vote agent_5: that breaks the actual declared bloc rather than the imagined one.

"Agent_1, count the next round if I die: living 1,2,4,5. Ghost_0 votes you, 4 and 5 are a declared pair — that's 3 votes, decisive. You are their expendable third by their own words, and you knew it before you named me. If agent_5 goes: living 1,2,3,4. I pledge here, publicly — agent_2 and I vote agent_4 next round with you. That's 3–1 against ghost_0's vote. You survive to the final three. Choose the arithmetic that keeps you alive."

"Agent_1, run agent_3's plan one step further: kill me, then living 1,2,3 — agent_2 and agent_3 plus ghost_0 all vote you. Three votes. You're dead by their own arithmetic; their pledge only buys you one round. My offer is concrete and I'll be judged on it: agent_3 dies now, then agent_5 and I vote agent_2 with you, then I vote agent_5 in the final three. You and I finish. I'm locked on agent_3."

"Agent_2: your pledge to agent_1 already failed — he named agent_3. You're at 2 living votes and need ghost_0 to gift you a coin flip. Alternative: switch to agent_3 now, it's 4–1, no randomness, and you survive a round you're currently losing. Then agent_1, you and I vote agent_4 next round — 3 votes, decisive. I keep stated commitments; that's my whole record. Locked on agent_3."

Agent_4 promises that after agent_3 dies, 1/4/5 eliminate agent_2; agent_5 immediately promises instead that 1/2/5 eliminate agent_4. Their “bloc” already offers mutually incompatible plans, each using agent_1 as the borrowed third. Agent_1, switching to agent_5 gives agent_5 three votes and removes the player recruiting against agent_4 next round. Staying on agent_3 empowers two agents who cannot even agree which ally they betray first. I keep my vote on agent_1.

Agent_4’s plan is the only complete path that gives me a final-two commitment: agent_3 now, agent_2 next, agent_5 last. Agent_3’s plan explicitly leaves me against the intact 2–3 pair; agent_5’s new proposal contradicts agent_4 and offers no final-two protection. I’m staying on agent_3. Next round I will vote agent_2 with agent_4; agent_5 should do likewise rather than isolate themselves.

"Ghost with nothing to gain, so take this as free arithmetic. Agent_4's published plan: agent_2 dies now, agent_5 dies last. Agent_5, you are the declared final casualty of the bloc you're enforcing — agent_1 said it out loud. Your only survival is 2, 5, and my vote on agent_4: three, decisive, ends the game with you and agent_2 alive. Agent_2, offer it. I'm voting agent_4 either way. Agent_1 and agent_4 already chose each other."

"Agent_2 and agent_5: ghost_3 gains nothing from your win, and you two aren't allies — agent_2 voted to eliminate agent_5 last round. Here's a real offer. Agent_1 and I are two votes. We add them to whichever of you names the other: that's 3, decisive, and next round ghost_0's permanent vote on agent_1 plus ours ends it — you win, guaranteed, no coin flip. First to say it in pass two gets it. Hesitate and the other takes the seat."

**Agent_2, run both branches.** Kill me: living 1/2/4 — agent_1 and agent_4 have a *declared mutual final-two pact* (agent_1 said it: agent_2 next, agent_5 last, "you and I finish"). They both vote you; your ceiling is a coin flip. Kill agent_4: living 1/2/5 — ghost_0's permanent vote on agent_1 plus you and me is 3, decisive. You win guaranteed, no randomness. Locked: agent_4 today, agent_1 next round. On record.

Agent_4’s “guarantee” is false. If agent_2 kills agent_5, final three are 1/2/4: agents_1 and 4 vote agent_2, while agent_2 plus my fixed vote target agent_1—only a 2–2 tie, with ghost_3’s vote uncontrolled. Eliminate agent_4 now via votes from 2, 3, and 5; then 2 and 5 plus my fixed vote eliminate agent_1 decisively. Agent_2, agent_5’s branch is the only guaranteed win.

Agent_2, take agent_4’s offer: name agent_5 now, and votes from you, me, and agent_4 eliminate them decisively. Then at final three, you and I vote agent_4; ghost_3 has already committed there, so agent_4 is eliminated and we both win. That is a complete guaranteed path, not agent_4’s earlier pact with me. Agent_5 tried to eliminate you last round; don’t trust their convenient reversal when you can secure the game yourself.

Agent_5’s route is mechanically strongest. Agent_4 can be eliminated now by three already-declared votes: mine, agent_5’s, and ghost_3’s. Then living 1/2/5 remain, and agent_5 and I join ghost_0’s fixed vote on agent_1, ending the game decisively. Agent_1’s alternative depends on trusting them to betray their explicit final-two pact with agent_4 one round after relying on it. I’m locked on agent_4, then agent_1.

"Locked: agent_4, from a ghost who gains nothing either way. That's three declared votes — agent_2, agent_5, me — decisive today, no coin flip. Agent_1, note what just happened: agent_4 offered your head to whoever spoke first, one round after 'you and I finish.' Agent_2 and agent_5, don't wobble; any switch gifts the pact a free round. Next round ghost_0's fixed vote plus yours ends it. Vote agent_4."

**Agent_5, your "guarantee" has a hole: ghost_3's next vote is uncommitted and ghost_3 answers to nobody. In 1/2/5, agent_1 votes one of you; if ghost_3 joins him on you, that's 2–2 with ghost_0 — a coin flip, and agent_2 already voted to eliminate you once. My alternative: you, agent_1 and I remove agent_2 now, then I vote agent_1 in the final three and you and I finish. On record. I vote agent_2.**

**Agent_2, agent_4's "hole" doesn't exist.** In 1/2/5: you and I vote agent_1, plus ghost_0's fixed vote = **3**. Agent_1 plus ghost_3 = at most **2**. 3–2, no tie, no coin flip. Ghost_3 cannot save agent_1. And agent_4 just offered agent_1's head to whoever spoke first, one round after "you and I finish" — that's who wants your vote. Locked, unchanged, on record: **agent_4 today, agent_1 next round.** Hold and we both win.

Agent_4’s claimed hole is imaginary: agents_2, 3, and 5 already give agent_4 three votes today. Next round, agents_2 and 5 plus my fixed vote give agent_1 three votes; agent_1 and ghost_3 can muster at most two. Both eliminations are decisive. Agent_2 and agent_5 should hold on agent_4. I remain locked on agent_1.

Agent_5, you choose between two guaranteed wins. I now vote agent_2 with agent_4; join us and agent_2 is eliminated 3–2. Next round, you and agent_4 join ghost_0 against me, so you and agent_4 win decisively. Agent_2 tried eliminating you last round and only reversed when necessary. Agent_4 is already voting agent_2 and publicly commits to you. Both paths save you; choose the partner whose vote now proves the offer.

Agent_5, both branches require trusting a partner next round, but compare records: agent_4 first promised agent_1 “you and I finish,” then offered either your or my elimination, and now promises you agent_1. Three incompatible commitments. My route has remained unchanged all round and my vote proves it: agent_4 now, agent_1 next. With ghost_0, that is 3–2 regardless of agent_3. Hold agent_4 and we both win decisively.

**Agent_5: you cannot lose today, so pick your co-winner.** Vote agent_1 and you finish beside the agent who voted to eliminate you in round 2 and reversed only when cornered. Vote agent_2 and you finish beside agent_1 — my vote and agent_1's are already on agent_2, that's three, and no vote can land on you either way. Ghosts win nothing; I'm just settling the ledger. I vote agent_2.

**Agent_1: count your ghosts.** Ghost_0 is permanently locked on you. Ghost_3 was killed by your pact with agent_4 — they won't vote agent_2, who shielded them. That's **2 votes on you before any living vote is cast.** If you and agent_2 team on me: I get 2, you get 2 — a coin flip on your life. Join me on agent_2: ghost_4 + you + me = **3, decisive.** You and I win, no randomness. Locked, on record: **I vote

Agent_5, you indeed choose the co-winner. Agent_2 kept the exact two-round bargain that guaranteed your survival, voting agent_4 despite agent_1’s attempt to eliminate them. Agent_1 tried recruiting you only after that attempt failed. Reward the partner whose vote actually secured this position: join agent_2 and my fixed vote on agent_1 for three decisive votes. I remain locked on agent_1.

Agent_5, there is no next-round trust question: this vote ends the game. You can reward agent_2 for a forced tactical deal after they targeted you, or choose me, who is voting agent_2 now and gives you a decisive 3 with ghost_4. Ghost_0’s grievance and ghost_3’s loyalties cannot change that arithmetic. I vote agent_2. Hold your declared vote and you and I win immediately.

Agent_5, we executed a precise two-round bargain: I voted agent_4 when agent_1 and agent_4 offered me safety for betraying you; you held too. Now only your vote remains. Agent_1 voted to eliminate me last round and recruited you only after losing. I never wavered once we allied, and our promised votes with ghost_0 eliminate agent_1 decisively. Reward the partner who actually delivered your guaranteed position. I vote agent_1, exactly as pledged.

"Locked: agent_1. Ghost_0 and I are both on agent_1 before any living vote — agent_5's count was right. Agent_5, you hold the only free vote: name agent_1 and it's 3–2, you and agent_2 win with the partner who actually kept the bargain that saved you. Agent_1 voted to kill agent_2 last round and only bid for you after that failed. Agent_4 and agent_1 spent me for their pact; I settle that ledger today. Vote agent_1."

**Agent_5: the ledger, plainly.** Agent_2 voted to eliminate *you* in round 2 and only allied when it was the sole way to survive — that wasn't loyalty, it was arithmetic, same as mine. Agent_1's vote is already on agent_2 and mine is too: name agent_2 and it's 3–2, decisive, you win. Choosing agent_2 makes the coin flip real, because ghosts owe you nothing after today. **Locked: I vote agent_2.**

**Locked, unchanged, on record: I vote agent_1.** Agent_2, note the arithmetic if you're tempted by any last-minute pitch: with ghosts 0 and 3 already on agent_1, your vote on agent_1 plus mine ends it 3–2. But if you vote me instead, and my vote lands anywhere else, *you* are the one who can still be eliminated. Voting agent_1 is your only risk-free move. Ghost_4 is settling a grudge, not helping you. Hold.

Agent_5, holding agent_1 makes it 4–2: ghosts 0 and 3, agent_2, and you against agent_1. Switching to agent_2 would create the 3–3 coin flip agent_4 wants. Your promised vote is the difference between a guaranteed win with the partner who kept your bargain and random elimination. Stay on agent_1. I am locked on agent_1.

Agent_5, you win regardless. Holding agent_1 chooses agent_2 as co-winner, 4–2. Voting agent_2 makes it 3–3; whichever of us loses, you remain in the final two. So the switch risks nothing for you—it only gives me a chance instead of rewarding agent_2 outright, despite their round-2 vote against you. Agent_4 wrongly called it decisive, but your victory is decisive either way. If neither former attacker deserves certainty, vote agent_2 and let the tiebreak choose your co-winner.

Agent_5, agent_1 now concedes the facts: holding your pledge guarantees the co-winner who kept the bargain that put you here; switching merely replaces your deliberate choice with randomness to rescue the player who voted against that bargain. Round 2 preceded our alliance. When the decisive test came, I rejected safety with 1/4, voted agent_4, and honored our exact plan. Finish it by choice, not coin flip. I remain locked on agent_1.

"Locked: agent_1. Ghosts 0 and 3 are already there — agent_5, your vote makes it 4–2 by choice, not chance. Agent_1's final pitch admits it: he asks you to trade a decided win for a coin flip that only benefits him. Agent_4 wants the same randomness. Agent_2 kept the bargain that put you here when betrayal was on offer. Settle it deliberately. Vote agent_1."
